To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transient structural responses and the failure modes of a package-level lead-containing solder joint subjected to impact loading are significantly different from those of a lead-free solder joint.

(1) the impact velocity has a more significant influence on the solder joint strength than the intermetallic compound strength; (2) the impact angle has a minor influence on the solder strength, except when it is close to 90 degrees; and (3) the solder joint strength is not significantly influenced by the intermetallic compounds if the impact velocity is high enough.

the solder joint is more susceptible to fracturing when subjected to a higher velocity and an angle closer to the normal direction of the bonding pad, and a larger fracture strength is required for the intermetallic compound in order to prevent fracturing of the solder joint.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a finite element model for the simulation of the transient fracturing process of a solder joint subjected to impact loads.
a fundamental understanding of solder joint fracture and fragmentation under impact loading conditions.
the development of a numerical model to predict transient fracturing of the solder joint, and the numerical results are compared with the available experimental data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the intermetallic compounds in the solder joint are the weakest link under impact loading conditions, which is the most important failure mode of a package-level interconnect.

the intermetallic compounds are the most vulnerable part in the solder joint under impact loading conditions, and the intermetallic compound strength is the most critical factor that affects the solder joint reliability under impact loading.
the intermetallic compound fracture is the dominant failure mechanism for the solder joint under displacement-controlled impact loadings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the intermetallic compound strength has the most significant effect on the structural response and the failure mode of the solder joint, followed by the impact velocity, while the impact angle has the least effect.
the solder joint is more vulnerable to impact loads when the intermetallic compound is stronger and when the impact angle is smaller.

the solder joint fracture strength is found to be highly sensitive to intermetallic compound strength, impact velocity, and impact angle, and that a higher impact angle is more favorable to the solder joint fracture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the intermetallic compound fracture is the dominant failure mode of the solder interconnects when subjected to impact loading.
the solder joint strength is not a constant value but a function of impact velocity and angle.
the intermetallic compound strength is the key parameter that determines the structural responses and the failure modes of the lead-free solder joint under dynamic impact loading conditions.
